The AgentOps strategy in Red Hat AI 3.6 is bring your own agent (BYOA), providing a sandbox environment for running agent harnesses through the addition of the OpenShell open source project.

In this article, I demonstrate the Omnigent project, a "meta-harness" for AI agents that gives a common UI layer over Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Goose, and others. You can swap or combine harnesses without rewrites, keep them in check with policies and sandboxing, and collaborate in real time on the same live session, from any device.

Omnigent can work in server mode so session data can be saved, shared between team members and forked, while preserving access to the underlying agent. Figure 1 provides an overview of the architecture.

While Omnigent can work with many sandbox providers, this article focuses on running it through OpenShell on Red Hat OpenShift to take advantage of BYOA. The documented path for Omnigent on OpenShell gives a basic integration, but for Red Hat OpenShift extra steps are needed. You can follow along with this exercise by implementing everything in my example GitHub repository, referenced throughout this article.

First, create a custom sandbox image using the components in the images directory in my GitHub repository, to ensure we're not exposing anything beyond what's needed. The requirements take compatibility and security into account.

Next, configure these OpenShell profiles and providers to load credentials (through OpenShell terminal or API). While Omnigent works with several different harnesses, like Pi and Goose, this exercise focuses on 4, to demonstrate how OpenShell standardizes credential injection and governance across diverse tools.

You can think of a profile as a snippet of an OpenShell policy, with a placeholder for a credential. The provider then adds that credential.

Use the script scripts/load-openshell-profiles.sh to automate the loading of these from your local environment variables.

Using Git, clone my Omnigent fork and modify the Kustomization overlay (openshift-openshell) in the branch scShiftShell.

First inspect server-config.yaml, which allows us to specify how we want sandboxes to be created, setting the image to use, an optional OpenShell workspace, node selector labels, and optionally changing the runtime class. This config must include the names of OpenShell providers created in the previous step.

Copy secrets.env.example to a secrets.env and adjust it to connect to a local OIDC server (for example, Keycloak). Alternatively, omit the OIDC values to allow the built in account manager to operate.

The integration of Omnigent with OpenShell is a comprehensive reference for the BYOA strategy of Red Hat AI. By integrating the OpenShell SDK directly, Omnigent can access the full breadth of OpenShell's features, without modifying agent source code.

The upcoming integration of OpenShell into Red Hat AI in 3.6 will add sandbox fast-provisioning, UX integration, the ability to choose the runtime class (like Kata containers), native multitenancy.

For Omnigent itself, there is a lot more to explore, like configuring MCP servers, how sharing of agentic sessions enables building Team Agents, and the many other ways in which you can connect to your sessions using mobile, terminal, and APIs.

The interface between Omnigent and OpenShell by design does not allow passing of files, only environment variables. This requires that the configuration files are present in the sandbox image when it is built, but can be tweaked with environment variables when required, as shown in the example for configuring LiteMaaS. This restriction creates a good separation of concerns, avoiding the inadvertent loading of files at runtime, even if it requires some more maintenance of sandbox images.

Inside an Omnigent host, agents are run with BubbleWrap, giving them further defense in depth on top of what OpenShell provides. This isolates the agent from the Omnigent host processes and the WebSocket it uses to call back to the Omnigent server.

While Omnigent remains a community project rather than part of the Red Hat AI roadmap, it exemplifies the power of BYOA. Explore our proof-of-concept repo on Github to test these sandbox policies in your own development clusters, and the OpenShell docs on security best practices.
